finite_default_domain.definition: Five singleton towers plus six non-adjacent two-tower placements on the native 5x5 grid: 11.
finite_default_domain.scope: Default native parameter distribution only; finite input count is not inflated by repeated sampling.

provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation:
In the original task, every blue (1) marker drops straight down its column onto the gray floor row. It overwrites the floor cell with 1, its old cell becomes background 0, and the pillar stays where it is.

The factory works out where 'down' points in the visible grid. A row-reversal does not change the vertical axis. Each clockwise rotation turns down into left, then up, then right. So d4%4 picks the fall direction: 0 is down, 1 is left, 2 is up, 3 is right.

The colour roles become constants: marker = palette[1] and background = palette[0]. The emitted program works directly in the visible grid. First it erases every marker cell to the background colour. Then, for each marker, it stamps the marker colour onto the grid edge of the same line in the fall direction: the bottom or top row of that column, or the left or right column of that row. This matches the archived solver's erase-then-stamp logic. The grid is not rotated and colours are not remapped.
draft_notes.limitations: The background is taken as the constant palette[0]. The archived solver instead used the most common colour; in this generator's domain these are always the same. The program assumes the floor lies on the grid edge in the fall direction and that markers are the only cells of colour palette[1], which the constructor guarantees. It works on rectangular grids, although the generator only makes square ones. The fixtures follow the uniform rule with no contradictions. I have not run any tests.
